content: Xylene refers to a group of three benzene derivatives, which include the ortho-, meta-, and para-isomers of dimethylbenzene. These isomers are distinguished by the positions of the two methyl groups attached to the benzene ring. Specifically, the ortho-isomer (o-xylene) has the IUPAC name 1,2-dimethylbenzene, the meta-isomer (m-xylene) is named 1,3-dimethylbenzene, and the para-isomer (p-xylene) is called 1,4-dimethylbenzene. Xylene is a colorless liquid with a sweet odor and is highly flammable. It naturally occurs in petroleum and coal tar and is also produced during forest fires. The chemical properties of xylene vary slightly depending on the isomer. Xylene has a boiling point of approximately 140°C (284°F) for all isomers. It is less dense than water, with a density of about 0.87 g/cm³. Xylene is produced industrially from petroleum and is one of the top 30 chemicals manufactured in the United States by volume. It is widely used as a solvent and in industries such as printing, rubber, and leather. Para-xylene (p-xylene) serves as a feedstock for the production of terephthalic acid, a monomer used in polymer manufacturing. Xylene is also employed as a cleaning agent for steel, silicon wafers, and chips, as well as a thinner for paint, and in the formulation of paints and varnishes. It can substitute for toluene in lacquers when slower drying is desired. Additionally, xylene is present in small amounts in airplane fuel and gasoline. In animal studies, xylene is sometimes applied to the ears of rabbits to enhance blood flow for collection, but the area must be cleaned with alcohol afterward to prevent inflammation. Xylene serves as a precursor for the synthesis of other chemicals. For example, chlorination of xylene produces xylylene dichlorides or 1,2-bis(chloromethyl)benzene, with three possible isomers. Oxidation of the methyl groups using agents like potassium permanganate (KMnO₄) can convert them into carboxylic acids. Oxidizing both methyl groups in o-xylene yields phthalic acid, while p-xylene oxidation produces terephthalic acid. Exposure to xylene can have significant effects on human health, particularly on the brain. Short-term exposure (14 days or less) or long-term exposure (more than one year) to high levels of xylene can result in symptoms such as headaches, dizziness, confusion, lack of muscle coordination, and changes in balance. High levels of xylene exposure can also irritate the skin, eyes, nose, and throat, cause difficulty breathing, and lead to lung problems, delayed reaction times, memory difficulties, stomach discomfort, and potential liver and kidney changes. Extremely high levels of exposure can cause unconsciousness and even death. Animal studies suggest that high concentrations of xylene may increase the risk of fetal death, delayed growth, and developmental issues in unborn animals. These concentrations often also harm the mothers. However, it is not yet clear whether low-level exposure to xylene during pregnancy poses risks to human fetuses. Beyond occupational exposure, humans may come into contact with xylene through soil contamination caused by leaking underground storage tanks containing petroleum products. Individuals exposed to contaminated soil or groundwater may experience adverse health effects, particularly if the groundwater is used as a water supply. Another common source of xylene exposure is through the use of certain pens, writing and drawing instruments, bingo markers, and art supplies.
